source_text: CAPUT UNDECIMUM. Eandem certo futuram esse, demonstratur e N.T. Vidimus Veteri Testamento clare satis adumbrari, praedicari ac promittere resurrectionem carnis certo futuram esse: nunc videbimus eam in N.T. tam perspicue doceri, ac si solis radio scripta.
english: CHAPTER ELEVEN. That the same is certainly future is demonstrated from the New Testament.

We have seen that in the Old Testament the resurrection of the flesh as certainly future is clearly enough foreshadowed, preached, and promised: now we shall see it taught in the New Testament so clearly as if written by a sunbeam.

source_text: IV. A spe, quam Apostolus connectit cum superiore; opponens opinioni perperam agentium certam spem gloriose patientium, & sicut ex illa, ita ex hac quoque resurrectionem confirmans v.30–32. dicit, nisi sit resurrectio mortuorum & spes retributionis, frustra fore se aliosque quotquot pro veritate & Christo extrema quaeque subeant. Cur enim, ait, nos periclitamur omni momento? Si secundum hominem, i.e. laudis vel lucri vel alia de causa, adversus bestias pugnavi Ephesi — contra homines bestianos, qualis Demetrius Act. 19 — quae mihi utilitas? Postremo, si mortui non suscitantur, non tantum frustra erimus capita nostra tot periculis objicientes, sed iis potius accedemus qui dicunt: edamus & bibamus, cras enim morimur.
english: IV. From the hope which the Apostle connects with the foregoing; opposing to the opinion of those who act wrongly the sure hope of those who suffer gloriously, and confirming the resurrection from this also as from that, vv.30–32: unless there is a resurrection of the dead and hope of recompense, he and all who undergo extremities for truth and Christ will have been in vain. Why, he says, are we in danger every hour? If after the manner of men — for praise or gain or some other cause for which secular men face dangers — I fought with beasts at Ephesus (against bestial men such as Demetrius, Acts 19), what does it profit me? Finally, if the dead are not raised, we shall not only in vain expose our heads to so many dangers, but rather will join those who say: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.

source_text: Ex omnibus opinionibus ista verissima esse videtur quae antiquissima, atque adeo quod ex Tertulliano attigerunt quidam praesumptione admitti debere, indeque Apostolum more suo ad hominem argumentari: quae etiam Musculi sententia est. Servatur enim simplex & usitata vocabulorum acceptio. Deinde certum est ecclesiam Corinthiorum non admodum puram eo tempore fuisse, atque ut Scaliger notat, tunc exitiabiles ritus & errores incepisse. Nihil igitur mirum homines tantis erroribus inquinatos circa baptismi administrationem erravisse. Si objiciatur quod Apostolus hunc abusum nullo verbo reprehendat: Resp. Chrysostomus — non ad ludicra respondendum. Articulus & non omnes sed quidam pro quibusdam baptizabantur; solos qui hoc faciebant notat, & de illis paulo post dixit v.34. Evigilate juste & nolite peccare.
english: Of all opinions that seems truest which is most ancient — and what some have gathered from Tertullian by presumption should be admitted — and thence the Apostle after his manner argues ad hominem: which is also Musculus's judgment. For the simple and customary acceptation of the words is preserved. Further it is certain the Corinthian church was not very pure then, and as Scaliger notes, deadly rites and errors had then begun. So it is no wonder men so stained with errors erred about baptism's administration.

If it be objected that the Apostle nowhere rebukes this abuse: Answer with Chrysostom — one need not answer to farces. The article shows not all but some were baptized for some; he notes only those who did this, and of them shortly after said v.34: Awake to righteousness and sin not.

source_text: II. A Dei providentia, per quam fieri nequit quin tandem piis & bonis, quibus plerisque in hac vita male est, bene sit, v.19. Et v.20 redit ad rationem primam. III. A baptismo pro mortuis, v.29. Quae ratio difficilis est & doctissimos interpretes mire exercuit. Primo Epiphanius haeres. 28. de Cerinthianis refert fuisse qui cum morte aliquis praeventus sine baptismo decessisset, sufficerent alium quem pro defuncto baptizarent. Secundo Epiphanius subnectit alios interpretantes de iis morti vicinis baptizatis. Hanc interpretationem praeferunt Calvinus, Petrus Martyr, Gualtherus, Hemmingius. Tertio Chrysostomus de Marcionitis abusus; exponit de confessione resurrectionis ante baptismum. Quarto Sedulius & scholastici de morte peccati. Quinto Bellarminus de baptismo lacrymarum ad purgatorium. Sexto Guilandus & Leidenenses de martyrio. Septimo Major de baptismo super sepulchris — cujus moris vestigium nullum. Octavo de lotione sepulchrali. Nono Camerarius. Decimo Scaliger de refrigerio annuo.
english: II. From God's providence, by which it cannot be but that at last it go well with the pious and good, to most of whom in this life it goes ill, v.19. And v.20 he returns to the first reason.

III. From baptism for the dead, v.29. This reason is difficult and has strangely exercised the most learned interpreters. First Epiphanius (Haer. 28 on the Cerinthians) reports some who, when someone died without baptism, substituted another to be baptized for the dead. Second, others of those baptized when near death — preferred by Calvin, Vermigli, Gualther, Hemmingsen. Third Chrysostom on Marcionite abuse; he expounds of confession of the resurrection before baptism. Fourth Sedulius and the schoolmen of the death of sin. Fifth Bellarmine of the baptism of tears for purgatory. Sixth Guilandus and the Leiden theologians of martyrdom. Seventh Major of baptism over graves — of which custom there is no trace. Eighth of sepulchral washing. Ninth Camerarius. Tenth Scaliger of annual refrigerium.

source_text: II. Estque inibi partim asserta, partim probata. III. Asserta est testimoniis divinae autoritatis. Nuda illius assertio in N.T. omnibus Christianis sufficit, quia ejus authoritas est divina & a Christianis merito recepta. Afferitur evidenter Joh. 5.v.28; c.6.v.39.40; c.11.v.24; Luc. 24.v.14; Act. 17.v.18 & 23.v.6 & 24.v.15; Phil. 3.v.21; 1 Thess. 4.v.14; 1 Tim. 4.
english: II. And there it is partly asserted, partly proved.

III. It is asserted by testimonies of divine authority. The bare assertion of it in the NT suffices for all Christians, because its authority is divine and deservedly received by Christians. It is plainly brought forward at John 5:28; 6:39–40; 11:24; Luke 24:14; Acts 17:18 and 23:6 and 24:15; Phil. 3:21; 1 Thess. 4:14; 1 Tim. 4.

source_text: IV. Probata est rationibus solidissimis. Etsi sufficiat nuda hujus dogmatis assertio Apostolica, tamen, ne quid desit contra negatores & sophistas, etiam probatur 1 Cor. 15 toto. Ratio I. Est a resurrectione Christi & conformitate conjunctioneque nostri cum Christo, tanquam membrorum cum capite, v.13. Resurrectio mortuorum, ait, si non est, Christus quoque non est suscitatus. Probatur consequentia: 1. Si nulla prorsus est resurrectio, neque Christus resurrexit, quippe qui unus fuit ex mortuis. 2. Ipse se vitem esse dixit, nos palmites, Joh. 15.v.5. & est caput corporis, i.e. Ecclesiae, Col. 1. Ex quo necessario sequitur, si juncta membra mortua sunt manentia, caput quoque ipsum in morte manet. Ex hoc eodem principio disputat Paulus 1 Thess. 4.v.14. Deinde, posito consequente, multa sequuntur absurda: vanum praeconium; vanam fidem; nos adhuc in peccatis; Apostolos falsos testes Dei; eos qui obdormierunt in Christo periisse.
english: IV. It is proved by most solid reasons. Although the bare Apostolic assertion of this dogma suffices, yet lest anything be lacking against deniers and sophists, it is also proved through the whole of 1 Cor. 15.

Ratio I. From Christ's resurrection and our conformity and conjunction with Christ as members with the head, v.13: If there is no resurrection of the dead, Christ also has not been raised. The consequence is proved: (1) if there is utterly no resurrection, neither did Christ rise, since he was one of the dead; (2) he called himself the vine and us the branches (John 15:5) and is head of the body, the Church (Col. 1) — so if the joined members remain dead, the head itself also remains in death. From the same principle Paul argues at 1 Thess. 4:14. Then, the consequent granted, many absurdities follow: vain preaching; vain faith; we still in our sins; the Apostles false witnesses of God; those who fell asleep in Christ have perished.
